newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajik rebel supporters refuse to disarm.
newsitem.headline: Tajik rebel supporters refuse to disarm.

text.p: Armed supporters of a Tajik rebel colonel who fought government troops for four days this week vowed on Friday not to give up their weapons, saying the troops were still around the colonel's headquarters.

Russia's Interfax news agency quoted the rebel brigade's chief of staff, Ergash Khasanov, as saying "our corps will not hand over its weapons" because heavy artillery and pro-government forces had not been withdrawn.

Rebel commander Makhmud Khudoyberdyev ignored a decree by Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov on Wednesday, firing him from his command of the brigade after fighting in which he lost control of a strategic town in the former Soviet republic.
A government commission was due to fly to Kurgan-Tyube later on Friday to oversee the surrender of weapons and property.
But Interfax news agency quoted a military source in Dushanbe as saying the trip would only go ahead if the commission received assurances of safety from the rebels.

On Thursday the defiant commander warned of fresh fighting if government troops failed to withdraw to Dushanbe. "Honestly, I think it could only be war," the colonel said in an interview in Kurgan Tyube, about 110 km (70 miles) south of the capital.

Itar Tass news agency said Khudoyberdyev was negotiating with a senior commander from Russian-led peacekeeping forces deployed by the Commonwealth of Independent States near his headquarters in Kurgan Tyube.

But there was no word on the subject of the talks. Moscow has played a low-key role but is concerned about stability in Tajikistan, which borders Afghanistan and is seen by Russia as a buffer against the spread of Islamic fundamentalism.
Khudoberdyev told Interfax on Friday that there was some shooting in the southern region but put the incidents down to "illegal armed bands which are robbing the local population".
Khudoyberdyev's house in Kurgan Tyube came under attack on Thursday from what the rebel leader said were government troops.

Fighting erupted between rival armed groups last weekend in Dushanbe, only weeks after Rakhmonov signed a peace agreement with Islamic opposition guerrillas aimed at ending four years of civil war in Tajikistan. The guerrillas are not involved in the latest clashes.
Khudoyberdyev joined the fray, moving his brigade towards the capital last Saturday. The colonel is politically ambitious but the motive for his latest mutiny -- his third in two years -- is unclear.

For his part, Rakhmonov blamed the unrest on a "third force" opposed to his peace deal with the Islamists and mafia groups operating in the republic, which is spread across the Tien Shan and Pamir mountain ranges bordering China and Afghanistan.
"Active agitation, led by a 'third force' against the Tajik peace accord, has helped to bring about this mood of revenge," Rakhmonov said in an interview with the Russian daily Izvestia on Friday.
Khudoyberdyev opposes the return of armed Islamist guerrillas to Dushanbe, agreed under the peace deal.
He used the issue to declare autonomy for his southwestern region around Kurgan Tyube last month, setting up a "Defence Council" to run it -- deemed "unconstitutional" by Dushanbe.
Western observers say also that rival warlords -- all nominally loyal to Rakhmonov -- are battling for turf in the republic, its economy shattered by the civil war.
